TTX.description: A discussion-based exercise where players walk through a simulated incident without touching real systems.

TLP.description: How widely this document may be shared: CLEAR, GREEN, AMBER, AMBER+STRICT or RED.

AAR.description: The report written after the exercise: what happened, the findings and the improvement actions.

EEG.description: The guide evaluators follow during the exercise to observe and rate each objective.

SMART.description: The qualities every exercise objective should have.

NIS2.description: The EU directive on cybersecurity for essential and important entities, including incident reporting.

NCCS.description: EU cybersecurity rules for cross-border electricity flows (electricity sector only).

DORA.description: EU rules on ICT risk and resilience testing for the financial sector.

ENS.description: Spain's National Security Framework for public-sector information systems and their suppliers.

IRP.description: The documented plan for detecting, handling and recovering from security incidents.

BCP.description: The plan for keeping critical activities running during and after a disruption.

IT.description: Corporate systems and data: servers, networks, applications.

OT.description: Systems that monitor and control physical processes, e.g. industrial control and SCADA.

CSIRT.description: A team that handles security incidents; national CSIRTs receive regulatory incident reports.

EPT.description: The organization's Exercise Planners, who design and run its exercises; each exercise's planning team is drawn from it.

EPM.description: Leads the organization's exercise programme as a whole: which exercises happen over the years, their resources and budget, and the follow-up of their improvements.

MSEL.description: Its purpose is to make every objective of the exercise evaluable: it plans the events that will prompt the decisions to observe, when they happen and what response is expected from each area. That turns the discussion into something measurable — who acted, how and how fast — and each inject’s expected actions become what Evaluators observe in the EEG. It’s the planning team’s document; players never see it, they only get the SitMan.

SitMan.description: The handbook Players get before the session: objectives, rules, roles and the scenario’s starting point — never the injects.

ATT&CK.description: A public knowledge base of the tactics and techniques real attackers use.

TTP.description: How an attacker operates; the MSEL references them as ATT&CK techniques.

GDPR.description: EU rules on personal data; breaches are notified within 72 h. The UK keeps an equivalent UK GDPR.

RGPD.description: The Spanish name of the GDPR, Regulation (EU) 2016/679.

CER.description: EU rules on the resilience of critical entities against physical and cyber disruption.

SEC.description: The US regulator of listed companies; material cybersecurity incidents must be disclosed within 4 business days.

NYDFS.expansion: New York State Department of Financial Services
NYDFS.description: Regulates banks and insurers licensed in New York; its Part 500 sets their cybersecurity requirements.

FCA.description: The UK's financial conduct regulator; with the PRA it sets the operational resilience rules.

PRA.description: The UK's prudential regulator of banks and insurers, part of the Bank of England.

HIPAA.expansion: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
HIPAA.description: US law protecting health information; its Security Rule covers incident response and contingency planning.

PCI DSS.expansion: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
PCI DSS.description: The contractual security standard for anyone that handles payment card data.

needs.intro: The first step of the design: why this exercise exists, what it must prove and within which limits. The scenario can't be written until this form is approved.

stepDescriptions.document: Identifies the document and how it must be handled. The TLP label travels with every copy.
stepDescriptions.sponsorship: Who backs the exercise and commits to acting on what it finds. Without that commitment, findings go nowhere.
stepDescriptions.triggers: What prompted this exercise. The trigger sets the focus: validating a new plan isn't the same as evidencing compliance.
stepDescriptions.needs: The evidence behind each objective: gaps from risk analysis, past incidents and AARs, recent changes, threat intel or regulation.
stepDescriptions.capabilities: What the exercise will test. Keep it to four or fewer so the exercise stays focused.
stepDescriptions.objectives: Up to five SMART objectives. Each one comes from a need, has a measurable success criterion and says what evidence to collect.

stepDescriptions.risks: What could go wrong with the exercise itself, and how you'll handle it.

msel.title: Master Scenario Events List (MSEL)
msel.intro: Build the session here: one simulated incident that moves through 2 to 8 phases, driven by injects. Each phase opens with a situation update and the key questions to discuss. Inside each phase, injects are the messages simulated actors deliver to the players: mandatory injects set the storyline at a fixed T+ (session time; scenario time moves faster, per the time compression), and contingent injects branch off it when an expected action isn’t observed, then rejoin it.

tabDescriptions.scenario: The exercise’s one scenario: the story Players are given and how session time relates to scenario time.
tabDescriptions.phases: The moments the scenario goes through during the session — for example detection, escalation, response and recovery. Each opens with a situation update read to the players and the key questions the facilitator asks; its injects happen within it. You need at least 2 so the scenario can evolve (scenario time can jump forward between them), and at most 8 so each one leaves time to discuss.
tabDescriptions.injects: What each simulated actor delivers, to whom and when. Every inject evaluates at least one objective through its expected actions. Mandatory injects drive the storyline; contingent ones are optional — the facilitator’s plan B, sent only if Players stray from what’s expected (or race ahead) to steer them back. Worth one where a phase’s expected actions are easy to miss.
tabDescriptions.coverage: How well the injects cover each objective of the needs analysis, phase by phase.
tabDescriptions.review: Submit the MSEL for review, then mark it ready once every mandatory inject is validated. A ready version is frozen: conduct and the EEG use it.
tabDescriptions.threats: Optional: who is behind the attack — one or several actors, perhaps working together: MITRE ATT&CK groups or your organization’s, copied from the library, or an unknown actor. Skip it if the scenario has no attacker behind it or doesn’t need ATT&CK; the injects can still be noise or have no ATT&CK. If you use them, define them before writing the injects, which attribute their techniques to them.

evaluation.eegTitle: 1. What is observed — the definitive EEGs
evaluation.eegBody: Each objective of the needs analysis gets one EEG: the sheet its Evaluator holds during the session. It lists observation points — concrete things that are said, decided or recorded in the room, or that don't happen.
evaluation.sourcesIntro: The points come from three sources:
evaluation.sourceCriterion: Success criterion — one point per condition of the objective's success criterion. Its wording is edited in the needs analysis.
evaluation.sourceAction: Expected actions — from the READY MSEL, only the actions that evidence this objective (the “Evidences” toggles under each action of an inject). Their wording is edited in the MSEL. When either source changes, “Update the EEGs” brings the points in line.
evaluation.sourceOwn: Own points — written here, for what neither source covers: a concern of the sponsor, a lesson from a previous exercise, a question the session must answer.
evaluation.scaleIntro: Each point is rated on the common scale:
evaluation.levelP: Performed without challenges — done as expected and on time, following plans and procedures.
evaluation.levelS: With some challenges — done and achieved, with room to be more effective or efficient.
evaluation.levelM: With major challenges — only partly done, late, with help or harming other activities.
evaluation.levelU: Unable to be performed — not done, or done in a way that doesn't achieve what was expected.
evaluation.scaleAdjust: Adjust a level only where a point has a clear threshold — a phase deadline, a contingent inject that had to fire, a minimum number of decisions — so that two Evaluators rate the same thing the same way. A level left blank keeps the common definition.
evaluation.whoBody: Every objective needs at least one Evaluator, and the Lead Evaluator coordinates them and consolidates the ratings. The people come from the exercise team; here you choose which EEGs each one covers and, optionally, which participating areas they watch, so that every area is followed by someone. Evaluators observe without intervening: they don't play, facilitate or answer the Players' questions.
evaluation.howBody: Choose the methods the Evaluators will rely on — direct observation, the decision timeline, the communications log, observation notes, review of the documents produced in the room, feedback forms, the hot wash — and add any other source, such as a live poll. Name the log keeper: a member of the planning and control team who records the session as it happens, so that times and decisions don't depend on memory.
evaluation.resultBody: Once the plan is ready, these EEGs are the ones the Evaluators rate with in Control and Execution, and the ones printed in the EEG and evaluation plan documents. Writing them now, before the session, is what makes the after-action report rest on evidence rather than impressions.

assistant.notice: Everything the assistant reads from TTX-Zone (your exercises' needs analyses, MSELs and after-action reports, with their TLP-classified content; what their sessions recorded, such as decisions, ratings, the team's notes and the feedback form's answers; and the catalogs) is sent to the AI provider your client uses (Anthropic, for Claude Desktop) and handled under that provider's terms, not TTX-Zone's. forwarding.title: Forward to a SIEM
forwarding.description: Every new entry is sent as it happens to your SIEM's HTTPS collector, oldest first: a POST with a JSON body {"source": "ttx-zone", "events": [...]}, each event with the fields of the JSON Lines download. Each delivery carries X-TTX-Zone-Timestamp and X-TTX-Zone-Signature (sha256= HMAC of "timestamp.body" with the secret below), so the collector can check it came from here. If the collector fails, entries wait and are retried in order. Entries from before forwarding was set up aren't sent: download them.
forwarding.descriptionHttp: Every new entry is sent as it happens to your SIEM's collector, oldest first: a POST with a JSON body {"source": "ttx-zone", "events": [...]}, each event with the fields of the JSON Lines download. Each delivery carries X-TTX-Zone-Timestamp and X-TTX-Zone-Signature (sha256= HMAC of "timestamp.body" with the secret below), so the collector can check it came from here. If the collector fails, entries wait and are retried in order. This deployment also accepts plain http:// collectors: use them only inside your own network, the entries name accounts.
forwarding.authorizationHint: For collectors that ask for a token (Splunk HEC, Elastic, a gateway). It's stored and sent, never shown again.
forwarding.secretHint: Give it to whoever configures the collector. A new secret takes effect at once: update the collector too.
forwarding.copyFailed: Couldn't copy: select the secret and copy it by hand
forwarding.removeWarning_one: New entries stop going to the collector, and the {{count}} entry still waiting is dropped. The activity log itself stays.
forwarding.removeWarning_other: New entries stop going to the collector, and the {{count}} entries still waiting are dropped. The activity log itself stays.

server.description: The address messages come from and the SMTP server that sends them: your organization's relay, Microsoft 365, Google Workspace or a provider such as Amazon SES or SendGrid. The sender's domain needs SPF, DKIM and DMARC records that allow this server, or messages land in spam.

Microsoft Entra ID may leave this out of its tokens: after a sign-in, its event in the activity log says whether it counted (provider_mfa).

assistant.title: AI assistant
assistant.description: Lets accounts connect an AI client they run themselves (such as Claude Desktop) to TTX-Zone with a personal access token. The client reads, as that person, the exercises they plan, the knowledge base and the catalogs; it changes nothing. Off by default.
assistant.pinned: The deployment's configuration sets this (ASSISTANT_ENABLED), so it can't be changed here.
assistant.operatorNotice: What a client reads, a session's records included, leaves this server for the AI provider each person chooses, under that provider's terms; TTX-Zone doesn't filter it. Check that this fits your organization's data policies. Every person accepts a notice saying so when creating a token, and every call is recorded for 90 days: who, which tool, which exercise. Instance administrators see each call here, but never what was asked or answered. Turning it off stops every token at once.
